steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on pedestrian trajectory prediction that combines a Transformer with an asymptotically stable dynamical system. Cover why trajectory prediction matters, how methods evolved from physics-based to deep learning and goal-conditioned models, the explainability problem, and what our framework contributes.

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Why trajectory prediction matters
  - human motion analysis needed for safe human-human and human-robot interaction
  - pedestrian trajectory prediction important part of it; used in autonomous driving, robot navigation
  - earlier: physics-based methods - social force model, constant velocity/acceleration model
  - recently: deep learning, thanks to public large-scale data
  - motion patterns from previously observed trajectories -> predict future movement
- Evolution of deep learning models
  - RNNs and variants -> Transformer models
  - problem modelled as spatiotemporal sequence for future positions
  - LSTM widely used for temporal + spatial information in different scenes/situations
  - Transformer-based: better accuracy than LSTM; temporal dependency directly, spatial information indirectly
- Goal-conditioned prediction
  - encoding goals (position or desired location) with historically observed trajectories -> notable improvements
  - reduces uncertainty: humans mostly walk towards predefined destination
  - approach 1: semantic goals (e.g. right-turn) via computer vision methods
  - approach 2: goal position from expert system or sampling in neural network models
- Limits of deep learning
  - state-of-the-art for forecasting human trajectories
  - black box, lack explainability: unclear why predicted trajectories have given shapes
  - limited a priori assumptions -> no explicitly enforced constraints
  - explainability + explicit constraints essential: analyze behaviour, attribute responsibility, engender trust
  - fix: introduce prior knowledge into deep learning models
- Our framework
  - dynamics-based deep learning framework: novel asymptotically stable dynamical system inside a Transformer
  - enforces trajectory to converge to equilibrium point = pedestrian destination
  - matches goal-targeted feature of human movement (Fig. 1); gives Transformer prior knowledge + explainability
  - also learns continuity, smoothness, boundness; temporal and spatial properties via Transformer
- Specific design and main contribution
  - goal estimator from Zhao et al. -> endpoint estimated in advance
  - STAR (Spatio-Temporal grAph tRansformer) learns asymptotically stable dynamical system suited to human motion
  - contribution: stable dynamical systems within a Transformer, trajectory converges to predicted goal -> prior knowledge, explainability

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Analysing human motion is needed in order to develop safe human-human and human-robot interaction systems. Predicting the trajectory of humans (pedestrians) is an important part of human motion analysis, and it is used widely in many fields, for example autonomous driving systems and robot navigation. Earlier research on predicting human movements started with physics-based methods, like the social force model and the constant velocity/acceleration model. In recent years deep learning models have become appealing for pedestrian (human) trajectory prediction, since large-scale data is now publicly available. In these approaches the motion patterns of pedestrians are taken from the trajectories of humans that were observed before, and these patterns are then used to predict the future movements of humans.

The deep learning models for this problem went from recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and their variants to Transformer models. Deep learning models treat the problem as a spatiotemporal sequence to predict the future positions. In particular RNNs like the long short-term memory (LSTM) model have been used a lot to represent the temporal and spatial information of human movements in different scenes/situations. The models based on Transformers have shown better prediction accuracy than the LSTM-based approaches, because they capture the temporal dependency directly and they capture the spatial information of human movements indirectly.

Recent efforts also found notable improvements in performance by encoding goals (position or desired location) in the deep neural network together with the trajectories observed historically. Encoding the goal information reduces the uncertainty in human motion, because humans mostly walk towards a predefined destination. One approach is to model the relationship between semantic goals, such as right-turn, using computer vision methods, to do trajectory prediction. The other approach is to use a goal position that comes from the expert system or from sampling in neural network models.

- Limits of deep learning
  - state-of-the-art for forecasting human trajectories
  - black box, lack explainability: unclear why predicted trajectories have given shapes
  - limited a priori assumptions -> no explicitly enforced constraints
  - explainability + explicit constraints essential: analyze behaviour, attribute responsibility, engender trust
  - fix: introduce prior knowledge into deep learning models
- Our framework
  - dynamics-based deep learning framework: novel asymptotically stable dynamical system inside a Transformer
  - enforces trajectory to converge to equilibrium point = pedestrian destination
  - matches goal-targeted feature of human movement (Fig. 1); gives Transformer prior knowledge + explainability
  - also learns continuity, smoothness, boundness; temporal and spatial properties via Transformer
- Specific design and main contribution
  - goal estimator from Zhao et al. -> endpoint estimated in advance
  - STAR (Spatio-Temporal grAph tRansformer) learns asymptotically stable dynamical system suited to human motion
  - contribution: stable dynamical systems within a Transformer, trajectory converges to predicted goal -> prior knowledge, explainability

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Analysing human motion is needed in order to develop safe human-human and human-robot interaction systems. Predicting the trajectory of humans (pedestrians) is an important part of human motion analysis, and it is used widely in many fields, for example autonomous driving systems and robot navigation. Earlier research on predicting human movements started with physics-based methods, like the social force model and the constant velocity/acceleration model. In recent years deep learning models have become appealing for pedestrian (human) trajectory prediction, since large-scale data is now publicly available. In these approaches the motion patterns of pedestrians are taken from the trajectories of humans that were observed before, and these patterns are then used to predict the future movements of humans.

The deep learning models for this problem went from recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and their variants to Transformer models. Deep learning models treat the problem as a spatiotemporal sequence to predict the future positions. In particular RNNs like the long short-term memory (LSTM) model have been used a lot to represent the temporal and spatial information of human movements in different scenes/situations. The models based on Transformers have shown better prediction accuracy than the LSTM-based approaches, because they capture the temporal dependency directly and they capture the spatial information of human movements indirectly.

Recent efforts also found notable improvements in performance by encoding goals (position or desired location) in the deep neural network together with the trajectories observed historically. Encoding the goal information reduces the uncertainty in human motion, because humans mostly walk towards a predefined destination. One approach is to model the relationship between semantic goals, such as right-turn, using computer vision methods, to do trajectory prediction. The other approach is to use a goal position that comes from the expert system or from sampling in neural network models.

Deep learning methods have shown state-of-the-art performance for forecasting human trajectories. But they are considered black-box models and they lack explainability, so it is not clear why the predicted trajectories have the shapes they have. Also, deep learning models have only limited a priori assumptions about human movements, so they lack constraints that are explicitly enforced when the desired trajectories are predicted. Explainability and explicit constraints are essential for autonomous entities, since they let the autonomous entities analyze their behaviour, attribute responsibility and engender trust. The lack of explainability and the lack of explicit enforcement of known rules for the desired predicted trajectories can be addressed by putting prior knowledge into the deep learning models.

In this paper we propose a dynamics-based deep learning framework, where we integrate a novel asymptotically stable dynamical system into a Transformer model. We use this framework to model human motion, and it can explicitly enforce the human trajectory to converge to the equilibrium point, which in pedestrian trajectory prediction is the destination of the pedestrian. This property fits with the goal-targeted feature of human movements, as shown in Fig. 1, and it can also give the Transformer model in our framework prior knowledge and explainability. Our framework also learns properties of human motion such as continuity, smoothness and boundness, and through the Transformer model it learns the temporal and spatial properties of human movements.

Specifically, we use the goal estimator from Zhao et al. to estimate the endpoint in advance for the dynamical system we propose. Then we use a Transformer-based model, the Spatio-Temporal grAph tRansformer (STAR), to learn an asymptotically stable dynamical system that is behaviorally suitable to human motion, so the future human walking trajectory can be predicted more precisely. To sum up, our main contribution is that we integrate asymptotically stable dynamical systems within a Transformer model to model the goal-directed motion of humans, by enforcing the human walking trajectory to converge to a predicted goal position, and this gives the Transformer model prior knowledge and explainability.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Human motion analysis is required to develop safe human-human and human-robot interaction systems. Human (pedestrian) trajectory prediction plays an important part in human motion analysis [1] and is widely used in fields such as autonomous driving systems [2,3] and robot navigation [4]. Earlier research on predicting human movements started from physics-based methods, such as the social force model [5] and the constant velocity/acceleration model [6]. In recent years, deep learning models have become appealing for pedestrian (human) trajectory prediction with the public availability of large-scale data [7]. In these approaches, pedestrian motion patterns extracted from the trajectories of previously observed humans are used to predict future human movements.

Deep learning models for this problem have evolved from recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and their variants [8] to Transformer models [9]. Deep learning models the problem as a spatiotemporal sequence for predicting future positions [10]. In particular, RNNs such as the long short-term memory (LSTM) [11] model have been widely used to represent the temporal and spatial information of human movements in different scenes/situations [12,13,14,15]. Transformer-based models have shown better prediction accuracy than LSTM-based approaches by capturing the temporal dependency directly and the spatial information of human movements indirectly [16,17,18].

Recent efforts have also found notable performance improvements by encoding goals (position or desired location) in the deep neural network along with historically observed trajectories [19]. Encoding goal information reduces the uncertainty in human motion, since humans mostly walk towards a predefined destination. One approach is to model the relationship between semantic goals, such as right-turn, via computer vision methods to achieve trajectory prediction [20] [21]. The other approach is to use a goal position derived by the expert system or by sampling in neural network models [22,23,19].

Deep learning methods have shown state-of-the-art performance in forecasting human trajectories [24]. However, they are considered black-box models that lack explainability, which makes it unclear why the predicted trajectories have the shapes they do [25]. In addition, the limited a priori assumptions about human movements in deep learning models mean they lack explicitly enforced constraints when predicting desired trajectories [10]. Explainability and explicit constraints are essential for autonomous entities, since they allow autonomous entities to analyze their behaviour, attribute responsibility, and engender trust [26]. The lack of explainability and of explicit enforcement of known rules on the desired predicted trajectories can be addressed by introducing prior knowledge into deep learning models [10,27].

In this paper, we propose a dynamics-based deep learning framework that integrates a novel asymptotically stable dynamical system into a Transformer model. We use the framework to model human motion, and it can explicitly enforce the human trajectory to converge to the equilibrium point [28], i.e. the destination of the pedestrian in the domain of pedestrian trajectory prediction. This property is in line with the goal-targeted feature of human movements, as depicted in Fig. 1, and can also provide the Transformer model in our framework with prior knowledge and explainability. In addition, our framework learns properties of human motion such as continuity, smoothness and boundness [29], as well as the temporal and spatial properties of human movements via the Transformer model.

Specifically, we use the goal estimator from Zhao et al. [19] to estimate the endpoint in advance for our proposed dynamical system. We then use the Transformer-based model Spatio-Temporal grAph tRansformer (STAR) [16] to learn an asymptotically stable dynamical system that is behaviorally suitable to human motion, in order to predict the future human walking trajectory more precisely. In summary, our main contribution is the integration of asymptotically stable dynamical systems within a Transformer model to model human goal-directed motion, enforcing the human walking trajectory to converge to a predicted goal position and thereby providing the Transformer model with prior knowledge and explainability.
